title: Data senior domain exactly once vs at least once
topic: Data senior domain exactly once vs at least once
question: What's the difference between at-least-once, at-most-once, and exactly-once processing semantics, and how do real systems actually achieve something close to exactly-once?
idealAnswer:
At-least-once guarantees every message is processed, but a message may be processed more than once, e.g. after a retry following a crash before an acknowledgment was sent

At-most-once guarantees a message is never processed more than once, but some messages may be lost, e.g. if the consumer crashes after receiving but before processing

Exactly-once means every message is processed once and only once, which is genuinely hard to guarantee end-to-end across distributed components, especially when external side effects are involved

In practice, true exactly-once delivery is rarely achieved at the network/transport level, instead systems achieve exactly-once effects by combining at-least-once delivery with idempotent processing, e.g. deduplicating by a unique message ID, or transactional writes, e.g. atomically committing both the output and the offset/checkpoint together

A strong answer gives a concrete mechanism, e.g. Kafka's transactional producer/consumer APIs, or a sink that upserts on a unique key so reprocessing the same message has no additional effect

Notes the tradeoff: exactly-once semantics add complexity and often reduce throughput, so many systems deliberately choose at-least-once plus idempotent consumers as a simpler, more practical path to the same end result
